newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain seen meeting deficit goal despite June data. [CORRECTED 17:10 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Spain seen meeting deficit goal despite June data. [CORRECTED 17:10 GMT]

text.p: Spain reiterated on Wednesday it is confident of meeting its 2.5 percent year-end central government deficit target, despite it standing at 1.7 percent of gross domestic product in first half 1997.
The deficit rose from 1.2 percent (corrects figure from 1.1 percent) of GDP in the January-May period.
"We are confident of meeting the target of 2.5 percent and this 1.7 percent (to June) is in line with that goal," Budget Secretary Jose Folgado told Reuters in an interview today.

Analysts were disappointed by the June data although some highlighted the fact that the global picture of the Spanish economy, in a recovery phase, suggested a good performance in terms of the budget deficit.

"The June figures are bad, but it's also true that from an economic point of view it makes sense they will meet the goal. If Spain isn't going to meet it, nobody will," said Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.
But other economists said a worsening in the central state balance raised some doubts.

"Up to now people were confident Spain would meet the three percent (overall public deficit goal). Although we can't follow religiously in multiplying it by two, the number could mean 3.4 percent for the full year and it could well raise some question marks again," said Gwyn Hacche, economist at HSBC in London.

The 1.7 percent only referred to the central state deficit for which the target for the full-year figure stands at 2.5 percent, while the three percent requirement refers to the overall public sector deficit, which includes social and regional government shortfalls.
In June alone the deficit on a cash basis was 269.4 billion pesetas versus 380.6 billion pesetas in the year-ago month.
That compares with market forecasts for around 200 to 250 billion, prompting analysts to qualify the data as poor.
"There is a small setback in the (budget deficit) reduction process, which (this month) came in higher than forecasts," said Giorgio Radaelli, economist at Lehman Brothers in London.
"The government says that in the coming months the deficit will shrink, but they have been reiterating that since three to four months ago and we are seeing very little (evidence)," he added.
Folgado reiterated this view.
"We've done our forecasts. Both on a cash and national account basis we will easily meet the target (of 2.5 pct)," he said after the June figures were published today.

The central government deficit on a national account basis takes into account accrued revenues and expenditures for a given period, while the deficit on a cash basis registers actual money movements during a given month.

Folgado said that later this year the effect of the change in the accounting method from a cash basis to a national account basis for interest payments on short- term bills would imply a reduction in the deficit of around 240 billion pesetas.
"This adjustment will be some 300 billion pesetas for full year. So far (to June) this adjustment has (impacted) as little as 62 billion pesetas" he said.

Folgado admitted that lower inflation, now targeted at 2.2 percent by the government for year-end, implied reduced GDP growth in nominal terms -- 5.2 percent, instead of 6.0 percent as forecast in the 1997 budget.
"This is causing some problems," he said. But it did not change the global picture.

"Our calculations show (the deficit to GDP) will be around 2.4 percent or 2.5 percent. It is more likely to be 2.5 percent. One year ago we needed some budget adjustments, but not this year," he added.

"It's true than from July onwards the deficit is likely to improve. If it weren't for the interest payments this value would be around 1.3/1.4 percent," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
